reviews.title: Hire a Behavioral Scientist and Fix Your User Experience
reviews.text:
Clue collects tons of personal data about my moods, acne, energy, and symptoms but does almost nothing useful with it. The Analysis section is a cluttered mess of confusing charts, dots, and filters.

I don’t care what percentage of other women experience cramps or what happens during the luteal phase. I want to know when I am likely to have acne, feel irritable, or have a great day based on MY historical data.

I want to open a calendar and know when to schedule family photos so my skin looks good. That’s actionable information. Instead, I get a bunch of scientific explanations and useless charts.

Clue, hire a behavioral scientist who actually conducts user experience research. Test your interface with real people and find out what they want to accomplish instead of assuming more scientific information equals a better product.

If I can’t find the information I need in two seconds, your interface has failed. Turn my data into useful, personalized predictions. That’s the entire reason I’m tracking it.

reviews.title: I can no longer trust Clue
reviews.text:
used Clue for about a decade, but I have finally deleted it. Over the years, its Apple Health synchronization repeatedly failed or worked only intermittently, leaving serious gaps in years of important menstrual health records even though all permissions and settings were correct.

While looking for another way to restore the records that Clue had failed to sync, I unexpectedly discovered an even more alarming problem in earlier years. Clue had repeatedly written duplicate period records to Apple Health. In some individual years, there were more than 10,000 menstrual flow entries.

I ultimately had to export my Clue data, remove the incomplete and duplicated records from Apple Health, and rebuild my entire history using another app. This is completely unacceptable for an app entrusted with sensitive health information. After this experience, I simply cannot trust Clue with my health data anymore.

I loved the insight and I finally had proper insight into my hormones and feelings after YEARS! 

Then BOOM, suddenly Clue requires a subscription to even connect the Oura ring to track. Removing almost all of the helpful features unless you’re willing to pay and leaving nothing for free users. It’s a shame as I always had an impression of clue that they were community driven and wanted to offer all women the ability to improve their daily lives by understanding their cycles- not just the ladies with deeper pockets. 

Very disappointing given I’d not long ago made real investment into the oura ring. Out of principle I am now looking into alternatives.

reviews.title: Encourages Abortions
reviews.text:
I don’t care if you agree because some people care about this even if you don’t. We thought we were pregnant and because of my age it would not be ideal. Because I was late, this app provided information about pregnancy tests and what to do if you have a positive pregnancy test. The first statement was  about how my healthcare provider can help me coordinate the type of pregnancy or abortion care I need. It also discouraged the use of a crisis pregnancy clinic stating that they don’t “provide healthcare and uses tactics to talk people out of abortions.” 

The problem I have with this is that there is absolutely no excitement or encouragement  for being pregnant. Instead the topic of abortion is the heaviest portion of the information. I want an app that gets excited with me about my pregnancies and doesn’t make me feel like I should consider an abortion. 

In addition, when you go to your primary with a confirmed pregnancy, the first thing they order is an ultrasound to visually confirm pregnancy. Crisis pregnancy clinics usually provide the ultrasound for free right there on the spot! So how is that not providing medical care when it a the exact same protocol? They do provide care and much more by letting you see your moving baby, letting you hear the heartbeat, giving you a visual look at the legs arms and body that you are told is a clump of cells.
